extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, translators, illustrators, and general readers of Cervantes/Don Quixote
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and authorial preface on the nature, tone, and presentation of Cervantes' Don Quixote, including advice for translators, illustrators, critics, and authors about preserving its humour and characterisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of incongruity between Don Quixote’s imagined world and the real world is the underlying source of the book’s humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work foregrounds the discrepancy between things as he saw them and things as they were. Examples: Don Quixote taking a venta for a castle; the humour depends on readers seeing the mistaken perception. Anti-pattern: smoothing over or reconciling the incongruity so the ridiculousness disappears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict prosaic surroundings to heighten comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean, prosaic, commonplace character of surroundings gives significance to Don Quixote’s ceremonies and vigils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations and descriptions should represent settings (e.g., a rude stone trough in an inn-yard) realistically rather than grandly; misrepresenting a venta as an elaborate fountain or castle (as Gustave Doré is criticized for) misses Cervantes’ point and lessens the humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sancho’s incongruity as comedic centre
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the humour arises from Sancho Panza’s incongruity in words, ways, and works with his master’s ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray Sancho so his plainness and practical outlook contrast with Don Quixote’s romantic ideals; maintain his drollery, curt comments, and earthy plainness as a deliberate foil rather than flattening him into mere buffoonery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uns‑miling gravity / grave matter‑of‑fact tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Cervantes employs an unsmiling gravity — a grave, matter-of-fact narrative voice — which is essential to his humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an apparent unconsciousness of the author (authorial invisibility) and a deadpan presentation of ludicrous events. Anti-patterns: flippant, would‑be facetious styles or overt self-conscious jokiness (e.g., Motteux’s flippant version) which betray the author’s presence and spoil the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial invisibility (avoid self-conscious humour)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should keep himself out of sight; the humour depends on leaving the reader alone with the characters rather than on the author announcing comic intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subtle, non-self-referential narration. Contrast with Sterne-type self-conscious humour where 'the man' watches you over the shoulder — Cervantes avoids that; translators/adapters should try to preserve this restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve Spanish sonorous gravity in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Spanish has a natural gravity and sonorous stateliness that make absurdities doubly absurd; this quality is central to Sancho’s drollery and Cervantes’ humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators should attempt (recognizing limits) to retain the gravity and sonority of the original; expect some inevitable loss of flavour but avoid translating into a jaunty or frivolous register that undermines the humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coarse buffoonery and jocular excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Coarse buffoonery or deliberate clowning is out of place in attempting to represent Cervantes’ humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce characters to slapstick caricature; Sancho’s humour is comic through incongruity and gravity, not through exaggerated buffoonery. Anti-pattern: resorting to overt farce when subtle contrast suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical restraint: avoid extravagant eulogies and phantom readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should not substitute screams, strings of superlatives, or pompous epithets for sober perception; craze-based readings invent qualities not present in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate by identifying the qualities ordinary readers value (humour, humane characterisation) rather than inflating claims. Beware of seeing 'phantoms'—attributing nonexistent ideas or intentions to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise the book’s moral and reflective dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Don Quixote is not merely humorous; it contains essays, observations, reflections, and a mine of shrewd observation on mankind and human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should account for the book’s blend of humour with wisdom and social observation; it is rich in individualised character and serious reflection as well as comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied humour across registers
rubrics_metrics.description: The humour of Don Quixote ranges from broad farce to comedy as subtle as Shakespeare’s or Molière’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise and preserve the multiplicity of comic modes — from slapstick episodes to nuanced irony — and the way they naturalise the book across languages and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial erudition and pretence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Preface argues against padding a book with sonnets, epigrams, marginal quotations, and catalogues of authorities merely to appear learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial virtue: do not rely on borrowed authorities, fake annotations, or a catalogue of names to confer legitimacy. Anti-pattern: fabricating dedications, false sonnets, or marginal citations to feign scholarship (the friend’s ‘remedies’ show how easily this is faked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: musical, pleasant, plain, clear diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Style and diction should run musically, pleasantly, and plainly, with clear, proper, and well-placed words; ideas must be intelligible without confusion or obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a readable, well-modulated prose that moves melancholy to laughter and pleases both simple and judicious readers. Avoid convoluted conceits, obscure allusions, or overwrought rhetoric that obscure intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for broad audience responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The work should be written so that 'the simple shall not be wearied, that the judicious shall admire the invention, that the grave shall not despise it, nor the wise fail to praise it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance accessibility and depth: craft the narrative to engage a wide spectrum of readers without pandering or losing intellectual substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualised characterisation and broad humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Every character, however minor, should display life and individuality; the book should show a broad humanity (not a hateful one among them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid lay figures or flat stereotypes; give even minor characters distinguishing traits. Even morally doubtful characters (e.g., Maritornes) should be rendered with humane touches so readers can find some resemblance to Christian/ human feeling.
